conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived. We’ll use a short tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s just ten questions about the past week, and it helps us see whether you might be dealing with something more than the “baby blues.” Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinicians on your team. There are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself feeling able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*smiles faintly*  
“Honestly… not that often. I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but most of the time I’m too tired or pre-occupied with the baby to even notice. Maybe once or twice this week?”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly “no, not much”… I did chuckle once when my partner made a goofy face at the baby, but it felt kind of forced. I just haven’t felt that light-hearted spark I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

“Not really… I mean, I still plan things—like taking the stroller to the farmers’ market—but it feels more like a chore I ‘should’ do than something I’m excited about. I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to something for myself.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I wasn’t holding her “right.” My partner said she was probably just having an off day, but I still felt like it had to be something I did.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

“Yes… I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s stopped breathing—even though the monitor’s quiet and she’s right there. It’s like my brain invents catastrophes out of nowhere. Happens most days.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week—like yesterday afternoon. I was just folding laundry and suddenly felt this wave of dread, like something awful was about to happen. My chest got tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had to set the basket down and go check the baby even though she was napping fine. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

“Yes, most days. Between feedings every three hours, trying to sleep in tiny bursts, and the piles of laundry and dishes, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I’ll think, ‘Today I’ll shower and answer those texts,’ and suddenly it’s dinnertime and I’m still in pajamas with milk stains down the front. It’s not hopeless—just… overwhelming.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m miserable, but my mind just won’t settle once I lie down. I keep replaying every little thing—did I burp her long enough, did I fasten the car seat right—and by the time I stop spinning, the baby’s ready to eat again. I probably drift off around 3 a.m. and then she’s up at five, so I’m getting these broken little chunks of sleep most nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… it comes and goes. I’ll be fine for a few hours—maybe even smile at her little yawns—and then this heavy, weepy feeling just drops on me out of nowhere. I cried once yesterday while I was changing her diaper, not even sure why. It’s not every minute, but it’s definitely been hovering most days this week.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Only once this week. It was the night before last—she wouldn’t settle after the two-a.m. feed, and I just sat in the glider with tears rolling down while I rocked her. I wasn’t sobbing, more like quiet leaking, but it felt like the sadness was leaking out too.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and weepy, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and joyless-laughing feels forced, activities you used to enjoy now feel like chores, and waves of sadness or anxiety arrive without warning. Even when your baby is peacefully asleep, your mind races with worries about her safety and your ability to parent "correctly," leaving you with only broken hours of sleep and a constant sense of being overwhelmed.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports mostly "no, not much" laughter, only a single forced chuckle, and loss of previous light-heartedness, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal to no anticipatory enjoyment; activities feel obligatory and devoid of personal excitement, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring multiple times, specifically connecting the baby's fussiness to her own actions, consistent with "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense, and unprovoked anxiety episodes occurring "most days," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two clear panic-like episodes with physical symptoms (chest tightness, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and inability to complete basic tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep linked to anxious rumination, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, unpredictable waves of sadness and crying spells occurring most days, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total 19 (≥14 indicates probable major depressive episode). <sym>Anhedonia</sym> and <sym>low mood</sym> dominate (Q1-2 scored 2 and 3), with co-occurring <sym>generalised anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic symptoms</sym> (Q4-5 scored 3 and 2). <sym>Self-blame</sym>, <sym>overwhelm</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> not explained solely by infant needs align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No self-harm ideation (Q10 = 0) is reassuring yet severity warrants urgent follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1.  Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> this week
2.  Discuss medication and evidence-based therapy options (CBT, IPT) safe for breastfeeding
3.  Encourage 15-20 min outdoor daylight walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to lengthen sleep blocks
4.  Share EPDS result with your OB/midwife at the 6-week visit; request repeat screen in 2 weeks
5.  Keep local 24-h crisis line handy if distress escalates; bring support person to appointments
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___________  Source: self-report  Gestation/PP: ______ wks postpartum  Screening tool: EPDS (10-item self-rating)

Symptoms endorsed (≥3 days/week unless noted):  
- Markedly reduced ability to laugh or enjoy activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Recurrent, unexplained sadness/tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care (Q3)  
- Anxiety/panic attacks with physiological symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Persistent "racing mind" preventing sleep even when infant settled (Q7)  
- Daily sense of being overwhelmed and unable to complete basic tasks (Q6)

Patterns:  
- Anhedonia and low mood predominate; anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 equivalent) co-occur.  
- Sleep disruption is mood-driven, not solely infant schedule–related.  
- No cognitive distortions of self-harm; no suicidal ideation (Q10 = 0).

Screening significance:  
EPDS total ≥ likely 12–13 (provisional; formal scoring needed). Meets screening threshold for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety (postpartum onset). Moderate-severity; impairment in sleep, self-care, and parenting confidence.

Risk factors noted:  
- Primiparous, fragmented sleep ≤ 4 h nightly  
- Lack of perceived social reinforcement ("should" vs. want)  
- Acute panic episodes (tight chest, breathlessness)  
- Absence of self-harm intent (protective factor)

Safety: Denies self-harm or thoughts of harming infant. No psychotic features.

Recommendation:  
Refer for immediate clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, Edinburgh follow-up) to confirm severity and determine level-of-care (outpatient therapy vs. medication evaluation). Provide psycho-education, emergency contacts, and support resources today.
